input: Okay, so I finally finished the book my sister kept pushing on me, it's called The Sunday Kitchen by Marguerite Vance, and I want to get my thoughts down before I lose them. It came out in March of 2019, which I didn't realize, because I thought it was much newer. Anyway, the whole premise is that you spend about three hours on a Sunday cooking for the week, and she lays out this system of batch roasting, grain bases, and sauces you can rotate. What got me first was the chapter on containers. I expected a boring section about glass versus plastic, and instead she talks about labeling everything with the day you made it, not the day you'll eat it. That sounds small, but I've been throwing out mystery tupperware for years, so I actually laughed out loud. The part I'm still chewing on is her argument about decision fatigue. She says the real reason most people stop meal prepping is not that they run out of time, it's that by Wednesday they're tired of looking at the same chicken. Her fix is to prep components rather than full meals. Roast a tray of sweet potatoes, cook a pot of farro, make two dressings, and then assemble differently each night. I tried this last weekend, or I mean, I tried a version of it, because I didn't have farro, so I used brown rice from the back of the pantry, which was fine. I'm not totally sold on everything. Her grocery lists assume you have a stocked spice cabinet and a second fridge, and I definitely do not have a second fridge. There's a whole chapter on freezer stock that felt like it was written for a family of six in a house with a basement. I skimmed most of it. Honestly, that's the one place where I felt the book stopped being useful for someone in a studio apartment. But the core idea landed. Last Sunday I made a pan of lentils with cumin and lemon, a tray of roasted carrots, and a jar of tahini sauce that I thought would go bad and didn't. On Tuesday I had a bowl with all three plus a fried egg, and it felt like cooking, not like eating a sad Tupperware lunch. That's the whole win for me. So would I recommend it? Yes, with a caveat. Skip the freezer chapter unless you actually have the freezer space. Read the container section, because it's worth it. And if you're someone who keeps throwing out food, start with the labeling system alone, and see what happens. I think I'll make the lentils again this Sunday. Maybe I'll try the farro this time, if I remember to buy it. Okay, that's it for me, thanks for listening.

input: Okay, so this is the voice note for the parcel tracking tool we use at the warehouse, and the problem is that parcel PX-44871 has shown as "in transit" for nine days now. It was supposed to reach the Leeds depot on Monday the fourteenth of March, and it never did. Nobody has scanned it since the Thursday before, which was the sixth. The software is called RouteLog, version 3.8, and it pulls scan events from the courier's API every two hours. The client, Harlow & Finch Components, is asking us daily where their order is, so I need to get this sorted today. First thing I checked was whether the parcel was ever actually handed over. The courier's dispatch sheet for the sixth shows the consignment was loaded onto van seven, driver ID 2291. That part is fine. So the parcel left us. The gap is between van seven and the depot. Second thing, I looked at the event log in RouteLog for that parcel. There are four events total. Created, labelled, collected, and then nothing. The "collected" event has a timestamp of 06:52 on the sixth, which lines up with the van. So the software received the collection scan, but it never received anything after it. That's the first clue that the problem might be on the receiving side, not the sending side. Third, I rang the courier's support line on Tuesday the eleventh. The agent, Priyanka Desai, said their system showed a scan at the Milton Keynes hub on the seventh at 14:20. That's a scan we never got. So the courier has the event and we don't. That tells me the data is being lost between their feed and our ingestion, not in the field. Here's what I've already tried. I forced a manual resync of the courier feed on Wednesday the twelfth, and it came back with zero new events for that tracking number. I also checked the API token; it expired on the first of March and was renewed, but the renewal may have only covered the write endpoint, not the events endpoint. That's my best guess right now. So next steps. I'm going to request a fresh token with full read scope from the courier's developer portal, and I'll re-pull events for PX-44871 specifically, using the date range from the sixth to today. If the Milton Keynes scan shows up, we know the token was the problem. If it doesn't, I'll escalate to their integrations team with the ticket reference, which is CS-208834. I'll also check whether any other parcels from that same feed window are missing events. If there are, this isn't a single lost parcel, it's a feed gap, and that changes what I tell Harlow & Finch. Once that's done, I'll update the client by three o'clock. Okay, that's it. Sign off.

input: Okay, so I wanted to talk about the book I finished last week, which is called The Walls Between Us by a writer named Harriet Lowe. It's not a long book, about two hundred and ten pages, and most of it is set in a converted terrace house on Carrow Street in Leeds. The narrator is a retired piano teacher called Margaret Okafor, and the whole story turns on her relationship with the man upstairs, a night-shift electrician named Denis Walsh. I'll be honest, I picked it up expecting something light. The blurb made it sound like a gentle comedy about a grumpy old woman and a noisy neighbour. It isn't really that. It's more about how small irritations build up until they stop being about the noise at all. The first chapter is the one that stayed with me. Margaret hears Denis's drilling at six in the morning on the fourteenth of March, and she writes it down in a notebook, with the time and the length of each session. Lowe doesn't play this for laughs. She lets you see how carefully Margaret has organised her days around quiet, and how little she has left once that quiet is gone. What I found most interesting is the structure. Each chapter is headed with a date, and the dates are the only record of time that Margaret keeps. By the middle of the book you realise she has been counting the noise for eleven months, and that she never once knocked on his door to ask him about it. That silence on her part is the real subject of the novel, I think. Denis is not a villain, and Lowe is careful about that. We learn he has a daughter who lives in Bradford and only sees her on alternate weekends, and that the drilling is often him trying to finish things before a court date in late autumn. You don't get a big reveal. You just get enough to make Margaret's notebook feel slightly unfair, and the book is better for leaving that discomfort in place. I did have some frustrations. The middle section drags, and there's a subplot involving a landlord called Pritchard that never really goes anywhere. I also wanted the ending to land harder than it does. It's quietly satisfying rather than moving, and I think I'd expected something bigger after so much build-up. Still, I'd recommend it, particularly to anyone who has ever lain awake composing a complaint they never sent. It made me think about my own building, and about how easy it is to let a grievance become the most important thing in your week. So that's my take. If you read it, I'd be interested to hear whether you found the ending as muted as I did.

input: Okay, so the post is about our back garden in Millbrook, the little plot behind the house on Alder Lane that we've been fighting with since we moved in, which was March 2019. Wait, no, it was April, April 12th, because I remember the movers got stuck in the rain. Anyway, the point is it's roughly eleven metres long and maybe six wide, and when we got here it was basically a rectangle of compacted clay with one sad lilac and a fence that leaned about fifteen degrees toward the neighbours. The first section should cover the soil. I want to talk about the soil test we did in May with Dr. Priya Raman from the county extension office. She charged us forty dollars and told us the pH was 5.4, which is way too acidic for most vegetables, so we spent that first summer adding lime. I'd say bags of lime, not tons, though honestly it felt like tons, because Marcus carried every one of them through the side gate. Then the raised beds. We built three, out of cedar boards from Hollis Lumber, each four feet by eight. Actually, I think they were eight by four, long side along the fence, but I'll check the receipt. The first bed went in around late June, so the tomatoes went in late, and the Brandywine seedlings from Greenleaf Nursery got sunscald the first week. I want a photo of that, the sad purple-brown leaves, because it's a useful lesson. Next section: the compost bin. Marcus built it from pallets in July 2020, and it's the best thing we did all year. We fill it with kitchen scraps, shredded newspaper, and the leaves from the neighbour's maple, which she lets us rake every October. Something like three hundred pounds of finished compost last season, though I'm guessing on that number, so maybe leave the weight out. Closing section: what I'd do differently. Plant the herbs closer to the back door. Put in a rain barrel before spring, not after. And thank Mrs. Okafor next door, because she's the reason the fence finally stands up straight.

Dorothy grew up in Shelby County, Tennessee, and she always said the secret to a good garden was patience and cheap compost. I'm going to quote her directly, something like "dirt wants to be fed, not yelled at." I'll mention that she kept a spiral notebook, a green one with a coffee ring on the cover, and that we found it wedged under the shed's back step. The notebook has planting dates going back to 1981, which is wild to think about. Then comes the clearing. My brother Marcus and I spent the first two weekends in April 2019 pulling out the crabgrass by hand, which was miserable, and we filled eleven contractor bags. I want to be honest here that we made mistakes. We tried to save one of the rose bushes too late in the season and it died anyway. I'll say that plainly and move on, because readers trust you more when you admit it. The next section covers the soil. We had a soil test done through the county extension office in Memphis, and the results came back slightly acidic, around 5.8 on the pH scale. We added about four cubic yards of compost from Hollis Landscape Supply over the course of May. This is a good spot for a practical tip: get the test done before you buy anything, because it saves money. After that, the planting plan. We put in tomatoes, two kinds of basil, a row of Swiss chard, and a stubborn little fig tree that Dorothy had actually started from a cutting in 1992. The closing section should be about what the garden means now. We have a bench under the fig tree, and I sit there most evenings with a cup of tea. I'll end with an invitation for readers to share their own inherited gardens in the comments, and a quick note that I'll post a fall update in October once we see how the garlic comes up.

input: Okay, end of day, Thursday the fourteenth of March. Quick note on the photo backup thing, because I finally sorted out the plan and I want it written down before I forget the details. The problem was simple. Everything lived on one laptop and one external drive, and the drive was sitting right next to the laptop on the same desk. If the house flooded or the desk caught fire, we'd lose about eleven years of photos. Nina pointed that out last month when she was helping me clear space, and she was right. So here's the setup. Three copies, two different kinds of storage, one copy somewhere else. That's the rule everyone quotes, and for once I'm actually doing it. Copy one is the original library on the laptop. Copy two is the external drive, which I've renamed Backup_A and set to sync every Sunday night. Copy three is the cloud. I picked a service called Parcelbox because it has a flat price and it doesn't compress the originals, which mattered to me. The cloud upload was the slow part. We have about 212 gigabytes, and my upstream on the Comcast line is terrible, around eight megabits. I started it Tuesday night and it finished this morning at about six. I didn't touch it the whole time, which was honestly the hardest part. Then I did the thing I always skip. I restored three random folders from the cloud onto a spare machine to make sure they actually open. The 2019 Lisbon trip, a folder of scanned negatives from my dad, and last summer's lake weekend. All three opened. The scans are the ones I was worried about, so that's a relief. Next steps. Buy a second external drive and keep it at Nina's mother's place across town, rotating it once a month. Put a calendar reminder on the first Sunday of each month. And stop naming folders "misc photos final v2," because that's how we got here. That's it. Going to bed. Tomorrow, the drive swap.

I'll call Dana Monday to confirm the in-service date, and then I'll order it Tuesday morning.

input: So, let me walk you through where we are with the leak tracker, because it's been a bit of a saga. Back in February, we got a call from Mrs. Okafor at the Oakmont Apartments on Calder Avenue, saying water was coming through the ceiling in Unit 2B. Standard stuff. Except when Marco tried to log the job in JobTrail, the leak report just vanished after saving. No error, no confirmation, nothing. The first thing we tried was the obvious one. We cleared the cache on the tablet and logged back in. Same problem. Then Marco thought maybe it was the photos, since he'd attached three large images from the attic. So he resized them and tried again, and the report saved, but the photos didn't show up in the record. That was weird enough that we called the vendor on March 3rd. Their support person, Tanisha, was really helpful. She had us update to version 4.2, which she said fixed a sync bug. We did that on March 5th. It helped with the photos, sort of, but the leak reports still disappear about one time in five, and it's always the ones with a location tag. I don't know why yet. Here's where I'm stuck. Last week we had two more reports from that building, and one of them never reached the dispatch board at all. Dana found out only because the tenant called her directly. That's the part that really bothers me, honestly. A roof leak that doesn't get logged is a roof leak that doesn't get fixed. So, what I'd like to do next is run a test. Marco's going to create a dummy report with a location tag, from the office, and watch whether it shows on the dispatch board in real time. If it fails, we send the exact steps to Tanisha with screenshots. If it works, then maybe the problem is only on the field tablets, and that's a different conversation. Okay, that's where things stand. I'll update the thread once Marco's test is done.

input: Okay, so the side project is a little tool for neighbourhood power outages. The working name is Lantern Ledger, which I know is a bit twee, but it's fine for now. The basic idea is that when the lights go out on a street, people currently find out in five different ways, usually by walking to the corner to see if the café across the road still has power. I want one place where people can log an outage, see what their neighbours have reported, and get a rough sense of when things might come back. I've been thinking about this since the storm on the fourteenth of March last year. We lost power in our part of Ashgrove for about thirty-six hours. The utility's website said "investigating" for most of that time, and the only real information came from a woman named Dolores Kaminski two streets over, who had a battery radio and kept posting updates on the street group chat. Everyone relied on her. That's the problem I want to solve, really: the information existed, it just lived in one person's head and one radio. So the core features, in rough priority order. First, a simple report form. You tap "no power," it records your postcode, the time, and optionally your house number, which stays private and only gets used to group reports by block. Second, a map that shows clusters of reports, so you can see whether it's your house or the whole street. Third, a status line per block, something like "reported 14 minutes ago, 9 households affected," and that's it. No fancy prediction at the start. The technical side I'm keeping deliberately small. I'm planning to use a single hosted database, probably Supabase, because I don't want to run a server, and a static front end that works on a cheap phone over a patchy connection. Offline-first matters a lot here, because if the power is out, your mobile signal may be flaky too. I'd like the form to queue reports and send them when the connection returns. I've sketched a rough timeline. Weeks one and two are just the form and the database. Week three is the map. Week four I'll test it with my neighbours, which means knocking on doors on the Saturday of the second of May and asking whether they'd use it. If fewer than a third say yes, I'll stop and rethink. The thing I'm least sure about is trust. Reports from strangers can be wrong, or deliberately misleading, so I need some sort of confirmation. My current idea is that a block shows "confirmed" only when three separate households report within the same ten minutes. It's crude but it's honest about what it knows. Okay, that's the lot for now. Next step is to write the outage-reporting schema and send it to Priya on Thursday to see if she spots anything I've missed.

input: So I finished the audiobook last night, the one about the couple who gutted their 1950s kitchen in Dayton, and I've been turning it over ever since. The author, Marisol Quintero, spends the first three chapters on the cabinets alone. Honestly, I almost quit there, but I'm glad I didn't. What got me was the chapter about the tile. She ordered forty square feet of hexagon tile from a supplier in Akron, the box arrived with the wrong grout color, and she spent most of March 2019 arguing with a man named Dale Pruitt who kept saying it was the customer's fault. I mean, it wasn't really about tile. It was about how she stopped trusting her own judgment for a while. Then there's the part near the end, where she says the kitchen wasn't finished until they stopped calling it "the project." That's the line I wrote down. Or, wait, I think I wrote down the one before it, about the window over the sink facing east so the morning light hits the counter at seven-fifteen. Either way, both lines point at the same thing: you don't get a finished room by checking boxes, you get it by living in it long enough to notice what works. I'm not sure I'd recommend it to someone who just wants a renovation how-to. It's slow, and the budget numbers are vague. But if you've ever stood in a half-demolished room wondering what you'd gotten yourself into, it's worth the nine hours.

The main idea she kept coming back to was that you should buy for the next three years, not for the spec sheet on the day you buy it. That sounds obvious, but most of us do the opposite. We see a processor number, we see a bigger number for RAM, and we just go for the highest one we can afford. She argued that the real questions are how you'll use it, how long you want it to last, and whether you can actually repair or upgrade it later. She had a segment on battery life that I thought was really useful. Manufacturers quote battery numbers from lab tests with the screen dimmed and nothing running, so she suggested checking independent reviews that run a real browsing or video loop. She mentioned a model she tested, the Corvane Slate 14, which claimed fourteen hours and got about seven and a half on her loop. That gap is exactly the kind of thing you miss if you only read the box. Her advice on ports and display was practical too. Count how many USB-C ports you actually use in a normal week, then add one. Check whether the screen is sixty hertz or higher if you scroll a lot, and whether the brightness is rated in nits, because a dim panel is miserable near a window. What I'd push back on is the length. Forty minutes was a lot for something that boils down to three checks. Still, I'm taking notes into my own purchase next month, and I'm going to run the battery test myself before I pay anything.

input: Okay, so it's Saturday, March 9th, around four in the afternoon, and I'm recording this for Dana because she's going to ask me tomorrow what happened with the breaker panel and I know I'll forget half of it by then. The power went out in the house about an hour ago, and it wasn't the whole street, just us and the Okafors next door. So I figured it was something inside the house, not the utility. First thing I did was walk down to the basement with the flashlight, the big orange one that lives on the shelf by the water heater. I went straight to the panel. Nothing was tripped, at least not obviously. All the switches were sitting in the middle position, which is never a good sign, but I flipped the main back on and the lights came up for maybe two seconds and then everything died again. So I know it's not a simple overload. Then I remembered that the Okafors had mentioned their service line was getting replaced last fall, and I wondered whether the crew had nicked something at the meter base. I went outside and looked at the meter on the side of the house. The seal was fine, the glass wasn't cracked, and nothing was smoking or buzzing, which I was honestly relieved about. I called the utility's outage line and got an automated voice that gave me a reference number, ending in 4471, and said a crew had been dispatched for the neighborhood. That part was a relief, though it still doesn't explain why only our two houses are dark. Back inside, I started thinking about the main disconnect. Our panel is an older Square D with a main breaker on top, and when I looked closer I could see the handle was sitting slightly loose, like it had been bumped and not fully seated. I did not want to touch the live parts, so I stayed well clear of the bus bars and only pressed the handle firmly to the off position, waited a full minute, and then back on. This time the lights came on and stayed on. Dana, I'm telling you this because I want you to know I did not go poking around inside the panel. I just reseated the handle from the outside, and I'm pretty sure that's what fixed it. Still, it's not something I want to just ignore. The handle being loose suggests the connection at the bus might be worn or the lug might be getting warm. So I took a photo of the panel label and the main breaker, and I'm going to call an electrician on Monday, probably Mitch Delgado, the one who did the kitchen wiring two years ago. I'll ask him to take a look with a thermal camera and tell us whether it needs replacing. Anyway, that's where things stand. Power's back, the fridge is humming again, and I've got the reference number written on the whiteboard by the back door. Let me know if you want to swing by Monday when Mitch comes. Love you, see you for dinner.

input: Okay, so this is the outline for the blog post about switching mobile phone contracts, and I want it to feel warm and friendly, like I'm talking to a reader over coffee. The working title is "How I Finally Stopped Overpaying for My Phone Plan." I'll open with a short story about my neighbour, Dolores Abernathy, who called me in March of this year, completely frustrated because her bill had jumped from thirty-eight pounds to fifty-six pounds a month without anyone telling her why. That's the hook, and I think it works because almost everyone has had that moment of opening a bill and wondering what happened. Next section is the setup. I want to explain the difference between a fixed-term contract and a rolling monthly plan, because a lot of people don't really know which one they're on. I'll say that Dolores was still tied into a twenty-four month deal she signed with a provider called Brightwave Mobile back in 2022, and that the early exit fee was going to be around ninety pounds. So the lesson there is to check your end date before you do anything else. The third section is the practical part, and this is where I'll get into the steps. First, find your contract end date, which you can usually see in your account app or on your original paperwork. Second, pull up your last three bills and look for price rises buried in the small print, because a lot of providers add inflation-linked increases that never get mentioned in the headline price. Third, check what the current deals look like for your data needs, and be honest with yourself about how much data you actually use. Dolores, for example, was paying for fifty gigabytes and was averaging about six. Then I want a section on negotiating, which I think people underestimate. I'll describe how Dolores rang her provider on a Tuesday morning, mentioned she was thinking of leaving for a rival network, and asked for the retention team. She got put through to an advisor named Priya, who offered her a plan at thirty-one pounds a month with the same data, which was a real surprise. The point I want to make is that you're allowed to ask, and the worst they can say is no. After that, a short section on switching, covering SIM-only deals, how to keep your number, and the PAC code you need to request from your current provider. I'll mention that the switch itself took Dolores about forty minutes, and that her new service was live by the following Thursday. The closing section should be reflective. I'll talk about how the whole thing saved her roughly three hundred pounds over the year, and how the real win was the confidence to ask questions. I'll finish by inviting readers to share their own stories in the comments, and to check their bills this week.

If I'm being honest, that alone would save most people twenty minutes, and that's the whole pitch. Second thing. A lot of parents don't know which documents they need. Birth certificate, proof of address, immunisation record, sometimes a custody letter. I want a checklist that updates as you answer questions. If you say you rent, it asks for the tenancy agreement or a utility bill from the last ninety days. If you say you're separated, it asks about custody. Nobody should find out on the day they're missing a document. Third, the deadline problem. Last year Riverside closed applications on March fourteenth and a bunch of families found out on the fifteenth. So the app needs reminders. Lots of families have a kid starting reception and an older one moving from year four to year five. Those are different forms with different deadlines. I want one dashboard, one login, and each child gets a card with its own status. Green when done, amber when there's a missing document, red when the deadline is under seven days. Fifth, the signature. Some schools still want a wet signature on paper. Others accept a typed name. I'm not sure which is more common in our area yet. I need to call the office at Riverside and ask. Probably free for the first year, then a few pounds per child per season. Parents will pay for peace of mind if it's cheap. Schools won't pay us, and we shouldn't try to sell them anything. Keep it parent-facing. Seventh, data. This is sensitive stuff. Children's birth dates, medical notes, custody details. We store as little as possible. Encrypt everything. Then build a clickable mockup in a weekend, not a full app. Test it on my sister, she has two kids and no patience for bad forms. Open question: do we start with one school district or go national? The third section is about booking the movers. I'd recommend getting at least three quotes in writing. We used Pemberton & Sons, who quoted two hundred and eighty pounds for a two-bedroom flat with a flight of stairs at each end, and we went with them mainly because their coordinator, a woman named Priya Desai, actually asked us questions about the stairwell and the lift access before quoting. Change your address with the bank and the council tax office, and set up mail forwarding through the post office for at least three months. Take photographs of the empty flat before you hand back the keys, and keep the signed inventory from the movers. Then, once everything's in, don't try to unpack the whole flat in one go. Set one room as the priority and finish that before moving on. The last section is the sign-off. I want to close by saying that moving is exhausting but manageable if you give it structure, and invite readers to share their own tips in the comments below. Okay, that's the outline. I'll tidy the wording when I write the full draft tomorrow.

input: So this is my reflection on the book I finished last month, which is called "The Quiet Rack: Building a Home Server You Can Forget About." I picked it up mostly because my setup had gotten messy. I had a old tower under the stairs running three different services, a Raspberry Pi that nobody remembered the password for, and a router I had never really configured past the default. Reading the book felt like someone finally handing me a plan. The author, Dana Okonkwo, makes one argument that I keep coming back to. She says a home server should be boring. Every service you add is another thing that can break at two in the morning, so you should be picky about what earns a place on the network. I wrote that down almost word for word, because it's the opposite of how I had been thinking about it, which was more like, if I can run it, I should. The middle chapters are about storage and backups, and honestly that's where the book is strongest. She walks through a three-copy rule, one on the server, one on an external drive that lives in a different room, and one off-site, which in her case is an encrypted bucket she set up in March 2023 for about four dollars a month. She also has a good section on testing restores. I had never once tried restoring a backup on purpose, and she argues that an untested backup is basically a hope. That one landed hard. Where I think the book falls short is the networking part. It assumes you already understand VLANs, and the diagrams are a bit too tidy for a real house with three access points and a smart plug that refuses to join anything. I had to pause and look things up in other places. That's not a dealbreaker, but a beginner would struggle. Overall I'd recommend it, with the caveat that you should read it with a notebook open. I'm already planning the weekend I'll rebuild the setup, starting with retiring the Pi.

input: Okay, so this is me thinking out loud about the dentist situation, mostly so I stop going around in circles. I need to get my molar looked at, the one on the lower left that's been sensitive to cold since about March. I've narrowed it down to two places, and I want to compare them before I call anyone tomorrow. The first one is Harbor Street Dental, run by Dr. Anita Kowalczyk. Her office is about fifteen minutes from my apartment, which matters more than I'd like to admit, because if I have to get a crown or a follow-up I don't want to fight traffic on the bridge. Her initial exam is ninety-five dollars without insurance, and she takes my plan, Delmar Health Select, as an in-network provider. I checked that on their website last Thursday, I think it was the eleventh, but I should double-check because the page was a little unclear. The second option is Crescent Park Family Dentistry. Dr. Samuel Osei runs it, and his reviews are really strong, especially for people who are nervous, which I am, honestly. The exam there is sixty-five dollars, cash price, and they said they'd bill my insurance but I'd be out of network. Hmm, wait, no, I think they said they're in network but only for cleanings, not for restorative work. That's a big difference, so I need to call and confirm that specifically. Let me actually do the math on the crown, because that's what I'm really worried about. At Harbor Street the estimate for a porcelain crown is around eleven hundred and forty dollars. My plan would cover roughly half after the deductible, which I've already mostly met this year, so I'd owe about five hundred and sixty. At Crescent Park the quote I got over the phone was nine hundred and twenty, but that was out of network, so my coverage would drop to maybe thirty percent, and I'd end up paying closer to six hundred and forty. So on paper Harbor Street is cheaper even though it's the more expensive quote. That's a weird result and I want to make sure I'm not confusing myself. Okay, so the tradeoffs. Harbor Street is closer, cheaper in the end, and has the insurance I already know. Crescent Park is better if I'm going to be anxious in the chair, and Dr. Osei apparently offers nitrous oxide, which I didn't expect. Honestly the nitrous might be worth an extra hundred dollars to me. I think my plan is this. Call Harbor Street tomorrow morning, around nine, and ask them to confirm the in-network status for the crown specifically and whether they offer nitrous. If they say yes to both, I book with Anita. If not, I call Crescent Park and ask them the same questions about their restorative coverage. Right, that's the plan. I'll send myself a reminder for nine a.m. on Tuesday the fourteenth so I actually do it.

input: Okay, so the problem is with the photo backup script I set up on the home NAS back in March. It was supposed to sync everything from the family laptops into a folder called Family Photos on the big drive, and then push a copy to the cloud bucket every Sunday night. For about three weeks it worked fine. Then in early April I noticed the cloud copy was missing all of the files from Dana's phone import, which is around eleven thousand images from her trip to Lisbon. First thing I tried was checking the logs. The script writes to a file in /var/log/photosync, and the entries for those dates just say "skipped, unchanged." That's wrong, because the files were definitely new. So I thought maybe it was a timestamp problem. Phones can write odd modified dates, especially when they import from a camera card. I wrote a little check that compared file hashes instead of modification times, and that found the files on the NAS, but the upload step still ignored them. Then I looked at the bucket policy. Actually no, wait, I should say the sync tool, not the bucket policy, because the bucket policy is fine. I mean, I think it's fine. I reran the upload manually with verbose output on April 9th, and it uploaded all of them without complaint. So the problem is in the scheduled job, not the transfer itself. My current guess is that the job runs before Dana's import finishes on Sunday nights, so it takes a snapshot too early. I'm going to move the job to 2 a.m. Monday and see what happens.

input: Okay, so I want to talk about the podcast episode I listened to last week, the one about the ice storm that knocked out power across the north side of the county for nine days. The host, Dana Whitfield, spent most of the hour talking to people who lived through it, and I think the reason it stuck with me is that it wasn't really about the storm at all. It was about what people did in the gaps. The first guest was a retired postal carrier named Walter Okafor, who lives on Linden Court with his wife, Ruth. He described the first night in a very matter-of-fact way. The lights went out on the fourteenth of February at about six forty in the evening, and by eight he had already moved the two of them into the front room because it was the only space that still held any heat from the fireplace. He said that was the moment he realized they'd need a plan, not just a candle. What struck me most was his list. He had written it on the back of a utility bill, and he read it out to Dana: water, medications, a battery radio, a way to charge the phone in the car, and a name of someone checking on them every morning. That last item was the one I kept thinking about. Walter's neighbor, a nurse named Priya Shah, walked over every day at seven with a thermos of coffee, and that routine became the structure of the whole ordeal for them. Dana also interviewed a utility spokesperson, Marcus Bell, who was frank about the restoration timeline. He admitted the crews had prioritized hospitals and water pumps, and that residential streets like Linden Court were not restored until the twenty-third. I appreciated that he didn't dress it up. So what I'm taking away is pretty simple. Preparation matters less than having a few people you've already decided to rely on. I'm going to write my own version of Walter's list this weekend and actually tape it inside the pantry door.

input: Okay, so this is me dumping ideas for the side project before I lose them. It's the noisy neighbour thing. I've been sitting on it since March, when the couple upstairs, Priya and Tomasz, moved into flat 4B and started doing what I can only describe as furniture ballet at eleven at night. The working title is Thin Walls, for now. I'm not married to it. The core idea is an app that lets people log noise incidents with timestamps and a rough decibel reading from their phone mic, then generates a short report they can hand to a landlord or a housing officer. Less a complaint generator and more a diary that actually holds up. Most people don't complain because they think it'll be their word against someone else's. So the log has to feel credible. I was reading that one council wants at least a fortnight of entries, with date, start time, duration, and a plain description. I think it was Sheffield, actually, not Leeds. I'll check before I put it anywhere public. The template should match whatever they ask for. Second idea, and I like this one a lot: a shared layer. If three flats in the same block log the same bass line on the same night, that's a pattern, and a pattern is much harder to dismiss. Maybe a building code, a little invite link you pass around the landing. Nobody has to use their real name at first. People could be anonymous to each other, but the aggregate is visible to everyone in the block. Third thought, and I'm a bit wary of this one: a gentle first-message generator. A polite note you can send upstairs before anything escalates. Something that doesn't sound like a threat. Priya seems reasonable when I bump into her at the bins, so the default tone should be friendly and specific. Something like, "Hi, I wanted to mention that the noise after eleven has been hard to sleep through. Would you mind keeping the heavy furniture moves to daytime?" Monetisation, quick thought: free for individuals, a few pounds a month for letting agencies who want a dashboard across their properties. Probably not for the first version. Keep it boring. Things I still need to figure out. Phone mic decibel readings are not very accurate, so I'd have to label them as indicative only. Background logging will eat battery, too. And privacy matters more than I first thought, because recording audio is a much bigger deal than logging a number. I'm going to store levels only, never audio. That's a decision I want to write down now so I don't talk myself out of it later. Next steps, I think: call my friend Ola, who does environmental health work and will know what actually holds up. Build a clickable prototype over the weekend of the fourteenth. And try to get five people from the Hollis Road block to test it, starting with the Okonkwos in 2A, who have been very patient with me. Okay. That's enough for now. I'll transcribe the rest of this tomorrow.

input: Okay, so I finished the audiobook on the drive back from my sister's place last Sunday, and I want to get my thoughts down before I forget them. It's called "Tile by Tile," by a contractor named Dolores Aranda, and it covers the eleven months she spent gutting and rebuilding a 1962 ranch kitchen in Tulsa, Oklahoma, for a couple named the Whitfields. Their budget was forty-two thousand dollars. They ended up spending fifty-one. What struck me first was how little of the book is about cabinets. Most of it is about permits and sequencing. Aranda is almost obsessive about the order of operations. You cannot set the countertop until the cabinets are level, and you cannot level the cabinets until the subfloor is sound. She says the subfloor problem is where most people lose their money, and she gives an example from March 2019, when they pulled up the old linoleum and found water damage under the sink that had been hidden for decades. That chapter made me think about my own bathroom. I've been putting off opening the wall behind the tub for two years. Honestly, reading about the Whitfields' moment of dread, when the crew lead Marcus Oyelaran called her over and said, "You need to see this," made me want to stop procrastinating. I'm going to book a plumber this week. Not someday. This week. The second thing I appreciated was her honesty about money. She doesn't pretend the extra nine thousand dollars was a surprise to anyone who'd done this before. She breaks it down line by line. Eleven hundred for the rerouted gas line. Thirty-four hundred for the custom range hood, which the Whitfields chose after a showroom visit in Broken Arrow. Two thousand six hundred for the electrical panel upgrade the city inspector required in June. None of it is glamorous, but it's useful. She's basically saying: budget for the boring stuff, because the boring stuff is where the real costs are. I'll be honest, though, there were parts I didn't love. The middle section drags. She repeats the same lesson about communication with clients three or four times, and by the fourth time I wanted her to just move on. And the narration of the final reveal is a little too polished. I didn't need the slow-motion description of the backsplash light coming on. Still, I'd recommend it. If you're planning any kind of renovation, especially an older house, it's worth an afternoon. My main takeaway is simple. Sequence matters more than style, and the unglamorous work decides whether the glamorous work lasts. I'm going to write that on a sticky note and put it on the fridge. Okay, that's it. I'll send the plumber's number to my sister later.

I'd decided on Tuesday that I'd call them today, so I blocked out the late morning and made sure I had my account number and the last three bills in front of me. The contract itself is a twenty-four month plan I signed in October of last year. The monthly cost is forty-two pounds for unlimited calls, texts, and twelve gigabytes of data, and I'm paying it on a card that ends in 4471. What bothered me was that I've been using maybe three gigabytes a month, and the bills have been creeping up because of an out-of-bundle charge I didn't fully understand. So the goal was simple: lower the monthly cost, keep the same number, and not get locked into anything new without reading it properly. I called the Northline retention line at ten fifteen. The first person I spoke to, a man called Dariusz, was pleasant but couldn't change the plan himself, so he transferred me to the account team. That second call took about twenty minutes, mostly because they wanted to verify the account with a one-time code sent to my old email. I'd half expected that, so I had the code ready. Once I was through, the advisor, Priya, pulled up my usage history and confirmed what I suspected: I've been paying for far more data than I use. We went through three options. The first was to stay on the same contract and drop to an eight gigabyte bundle, which would bring it to thirty-six pounds a month. The second was to move to a rolling monthly SIM-only plan at around twenty-two pounds, but the catch there was that the handset would no longer be paid off, and I'd lose the loyalty discount I've had since the second year. The third was to switch to a fixed four gigabyte plan on a new twelve month term at twenty-eight pounds, with a credit of fifteen pounds for the first two months. I chose the first option. It keeps the same term, which ends on the fourteenth of October next year, and it doesn't cost me anything to change. Priya was clear that the change takes effect from the next billing cycle, which starts on the first of the month, so I'll see the new amount on my statement in early April. I asked her to put a note on the account that I'd declined the SIM-only offer, and she read the reference back to me: NL-5530917. Before I hung up I asked about the out-of-bundle charges. She explained that a roaming data add-on had been turned on when I travelled to Lisbon in February, and nobody had removed it. She switched it off and said I shouldn't see that again. I'll check the March statement when it arrives to make sure. So that's done. Next steps are to check the April bill, and to set a reminder for the first of September to look at the contract again before it expires. I'm glad I didn't just accept the first offer, and glad I had the details ready. That's all for today.

input: Okay, so this is the walkthrough for the slides export bug we've been chasing for the Lisbon conference talk. Quick background first. The talk is on Thursday the 14th of March, and the speaker deck is generated from a Markdown source by a little tool our developer relations team calls deckforge. It's an internal tool, written by Priya Raghunathan about two years ago, and it takes the Markdown, applies a theme, and spits out a PPTX file. The problem is that when the file is exported, every slide that contains a code block loses its syntax highlighting. The code is all there, the text is correct, but it's just plain grey monospace. Everything else looks fine. Titles, bullet points, the speaker notes, all good. So it's specific to code blocks, and I think that narrows it down a lot more than we initially assumed. What we've tried so far. On Monday, Marcus thought it was the theme file. He rebuilt the theme from scratch, copying the colour tokens over one at a time, and the highlighting still disappeared. I mean, it did come back for one slide, the intro one, but that turned out to be because that slide had a manually pasted code block, not one generated from Markdown. So that was a false lead, and we lost most of Monday on it. On Tuesday I looked at the highlighter itself. We use a library called Pygments to tokenise the code before deckforge writes it out. I checked the version, and it's 2.17, which is current, so that's not it either. Then I dumped the intermediate JSON that deckforge produces, and the token spans are there. Every keyword is tagged. So the tagging is working, and the loss happens somewhere between the JSON and the final PPTX. Which points at the writer step. Priya's writer maps token types to run properties, and I think there's a lookup table that has a fallback. If the token type isn't in the table, it falls back to the default run style. Now, I was going to say the table was missing the newer token types, but I checked, and it actually covers everything. So scratch that. The fallback is firing for a different reason. My current guess is the colour values. Some of the token colours are stored as short hex, like three digits, and the writer might be choking on those and quietly defaulting. I haven't confirmed it yet. Tomorrow morning I'm going to add a log line in the writer that prints every fallback it takes, and run it against the Lisbon deck. If the log shows short hex values, we've found it. If it doesn't, I'm stuck again. So the next step is that logging run, and if it's the hex values, the fix is probably a normalisation function before the lookup. Marcus has offered to write that if it turns out to be the cause. We have about ten days, so I'd like this closed by Friday the 8th at the latest, so there's time to rehearse with the real slides.

input: Okay, so this is me going through the electricity options before I call anyone back, mostly so I don't forget what I found. I've been comparing three plans for the flat on Calder Road, and the decision really comes down to how much we're using in the winter months. The first option is the current tariff with Northgate Energy. It's a standard variable rate, which right now is 27.4 pence per kilowatt hour, plus a daily standing charge of 61 pence. Over the last twelve months our average bill has been around £118 a month, but that jumped to £164 in January, which is what started all this. The good thing about staying put is there's no exit fee and no paperwork. The bad thing is that the rate can change with thirty days' notice, and they've already sent a letter saying it's going up again in April. The second option is a fixed deal from Brightwater Power. It's a twelve-month fix at 24.9 pence per kilowatt hour, with the standing charge at 58 pence a day. On paper that's cheaper, and at our usage it would probably save us about £14 a month. The catch is the exit fee, which is £60 if we leave before the twelve months are up, and I'd have to switch by the fourteenth of March to lock in the price before their next review. I checked, and they confirmed the offer is valid until then. The third option is a green tariff from Lowfield Energy, which is a bit more expensive. It's 26.1 pence per kilowatt hour with a standing charge of 63 pence a day, so it's actually a little worse on cost than Brightwater. What it does offer is a guaranteed renewable supply and a small cashback of £25 after the first six months if we stay. I'm not sure that's worth it, honestly, unless Jess really cares about where the power comes from, and I think she does a bit, so I'll ask her. Doing the rough sums, Brightwater saves the most over a year, roughly £168 compared with staying on Northgate, even after you factor in the possibility of having to pay the exit fee if we move house. Lowfield would save about £90 a year against Northgate, and it's the only one that comes with the cashback. Staying put is the simplest, but it's the most expensive if the April increase goes through. So my recommendation is Brightwater, probably, unless Jess says the green option matters a lot to her. I'll message her tonight, and if she's fine with it I'll call on Monday, the ninth, before the offer window gets tight. I'll also make sure to ask them to confirm the exit fee in writing. That's about it. I'll send the summary to the shared folder once I've spoken to her.

input: So I finally finished The Lantern Ledger last week, and I wanted to get my thoughts down while they're still fresh. It's a novel about a woman named Marisol Quintero who applies for a records-keeping job at a regional water authority in a small town called Harrow Bend. The application is the spine of the whole book, which sounds boring, but honestly it's the most tense thing I've read in years. What got me was how much of her life bleeds into a form she has to fill out. There's a question near the start, something like "Describe a time you handled conflict with a colleague," and she spends three chapters trying to answer it. Every draft reveals something new about her marriage ending in March 2019, about the brother she stopped speaking to, about the night she quit her last job without telling anyone. I kept thinking, we've all stared at a box like that and wondered what they actually want from us. The author, Dolores Brennan, handles it so gently. Nobody is a villain. The hiring manager, a man named Teodor Vance, is kind in his brief emails, and that makes it worse, because Marisol can't tell whether his kindness is a signal or just manners. I found myself rooting for her and also wanting to shake her, which I think is the point. Toward the end, she submits a shorter, plainer answer than anything she drafted, and it's the best line in the book. It's just a sentence about showing up early and fixing things nobody asked her to fix. Reading that, I actually teared up a little, which is silly for a job application. I'd recommend it, especially if you're in the middle of a search right now. It made me feel less alone in the awkward, overthinking part of it. Anyway, that's my take. Let me know if you've read it, because I'd love to hear whether you thought Teodor was a good guy or not.

input: Okay, so I finished the book on home networking last week, and I want to get some thoughts down before I forget them. The author, Marcus Delaney, spends the first few chapters arguing that most people build their home network by accident, one router, one smart plug, one printer at a time, and then wonder why everything feels slow. I related to that a lot. My own setup grew out of a single Netgear box I bought in March 2019 and never really revisited. What I appreciated most was the chapter on the home server. Delaney walks through setting up a small machine in a closet, running a file share and a backup target, and he's refreshingly honest about how much maintenance that involves. He doesn't pretend it's effortless. He talks about the Sunday afternoon when his drive failed and he realized his backups had been silently broken for four months. I laughed, but I also winced, because I've had almost the same experience. The part that stuck with me most was his idea of writing down the network as if you'd have to hand it to a stranger. He keeps a plain text file with IP addresses, the admin login location, and a note about which device does what. I started one this morning, and it already caught two things I'd forgotten about. I'd recommend the book if you've got a closet full of cables and a vague sense of guilt about it. It's not a deep technical manual. It's more like a friend showing you around their messy basement and being cheerful about it. I'm going to try his backup test routine this weekend, so I'll let you know how it goes.

input: We mentioned in some recent episodes that a lot of important work that is now very relevant in AI normalisation and localization was done in the realm of linguistics and NLP. We talked earlier about a improvement to the episode generation pipeline that I'm looking at making involving a classifier to identify the Hebrew words, those which are Hebrew but are written in Latin characters, another one to convert those identified words into Hebrew characters, and finally a script normalizer to normalize the script with the added language tags for Chatterbox Multilingual, the TTS engine that powers this show. I've looked at some of the interesting work done by Dikta and other pioneers of NLP in Hebrew and I would have assumed that in a society like this where code switching is part of everyday life for many immigrants that all of these things would have been solved challenges. You can find plenty of interesting small models in Hebrew that are designed to meet these accessory needs. For example, a model for diacritic restoration, adding the nekudot to unvowelized Hebrew. But unless I'm missing it and there's a chance that I am I wasn't able to find a classifier that looked at English containing Hebrew words and specifically classified the Hebrew words. I don't think it should be such a complicated small language model to create, and I think it would be of lasting value to do so. So I'm looking at creating a synthetic training data set and training up a small model for use, whether it works in this pipeline or for future use. But I think it illustrates the surprising number of permutations you can have when you begin thinking about the way in which small language models can bridge the gap between different languages. One common one that almost fulfilled this need was language identification. This would be a small language model which identifies different languages, but the catch for this use case was that those languages were all in the same character set and Hebrew was not supported. You also have niche models that will transliterate Hebrew directly into transliterated English.

input: Okay, so I'm just going to talk through this out loud, because I've been circling the same idea for three weeks and I need to get it out of my head. The side project is a small tool for people who run neighborhood food banks, and the working name is PantryPal. Right now it's really just a spreadsheet with a login screen, but the bones are there. The problem I keep coming back to is that volunteers at places like the Eastside Community Pantry in Dayton are tracking donations on paper clipboards. Maria Chen, who coordinates their Tuesday and Saturday shifts, told me last March that they lose about forty percent of their perishable inventory because nobody knows what came in on Thursday until it's already gone bad. That number is probably rough, but it stuck with me. So the idea is simple. A volunteer snaps a photo of a delivery slip, the app reads the items and expiration dates, and it sends a text reminder to whoever is on shift when something is about to expire. No app download for the volunteers, just SMS. I want to test that assumption first, because I don't actually know if people over sixty will text back reliably. Then there's the question of who pays for this. I've been thinking about a grant from the Harlan Family Foundation, which has a deadline of September 14th, and they told me on a call in June that they like tools that reduce waste without requiring new hires. That's a good sign, but I don't want to build the whole thing around one grant. Technically, I'm planning to use a simple Postgres database on a small Fly.io instance, with a basic OCR step through an off-the-shelf service. I'm not going to build my own OCR, obviously. The hard part isn't the reading, it's handling messy handwriting on delivery slips, which is honestly most of them. For the talk itself, I'm thinking about framing it around the gap between what software people assume about volunteers and what volunteers actually need. I could open with the clipboard photo, then walk through the three pilot weeks at Eastside, what broke, and what I'd do differently. I'd like to end with a live demo if the Wi-Fi in the conference room cooperates, which, let's be honest, is a big if. I also need to decide whether to bring Maria on stage. She'd be great, but she hates public speaking, so maybe a recorded clip with her permission. I'll ask her this week. Open questions I keep writing down: What's the minimum viable reminder? Do we need a second pantry before we can say anything about generalizing? And am I overthinking the OCR accuracy numbers? Probably yes. Okay, I think that's the core of it. I'll sort this into a proper outline tomorrow morning and send Maria a message tonight.

input: Okay, so I finally finished the book my sister gave me for my birthday, and I wanted to talk through it before I forget what I was thinking. It's called The Long Table, by a writer named Marisol Vance, and it's basically a novel built around one birthday party in a small town in Ohio. The party is for a woman named Ruth Halloran who turns seventy on a Saturday in late October, 2019, and the whole book takes place over about six hours. What got me is how ordinary the setup is. Nobody dies, nobody runs off with anyone, there's no big twist. It's just a folding table in a church basement, a sheet cake from the Kroger bakery that says "Happy 70th Ruth" with the R a little crooked, and about fourteen people who have known each other for decades and mostly have things they haven't said. I mean, that's the whole plot, and somehow I couldn't put it down. The chapter I keep thinking about is the one told from the point of view of Ruth's son, Daniel. He's standing by the coffee urn, and he's trying to decide whether to bring up the fact that the family farm was sold in March. Or, no, wait, it was sold in June, I checked, and that detail matters because he's been carrying it around since summer. He doesn't say anything. He just refills everyone's cups, and the author spends four pages on that one refill. It sounds boring when I describe it, but it wasn't. I think the reason it landed for me is that birthday parties are these weirdly honest events. Everyone is performing being happy for an hour, and underneath that you can see who's worn out, who's angry, who's been quietly keeping score. Vance understands that, and she doesn't rush it. I'd give it four stars, maybe four and a half. The middle drags a little, around the section with the raffle, and I didn't need the subplot about the parish secretary. But the ending, where the candles finally get blown out and nobody quite knows what to wish for, that one got me. I'd recommend it, especially if you've ever sat through a party you didn't really want to be at.

I mean, that's the whole plot, and somehow I couldn't put it down.

He's standing by the coffee urn, and he's trying to decide whether to bring up the fact that the family farm was sold in March. He just refills everyone's cups, and the author spends four pages on that one refill. It sounds boring when I describe it, but it wasn't.

I think the reason it landed for me is that birthday parties are these weirdly honest events. Everyone is performing being happy for an hour, and underneath that you can see who's worn out, who's angry, who's been quietly keeping score. Vance understands that, and she doesn't rush it.

I'd give it four stars, maybe four and a half. The middle drags a little, around the section with the raffle, and I didn't need the subplot about the parish secretary. But the ending, where the candles finally get blown out and nobody quite knows what to wish for, that one got me. I'd recommend it, especially if you've ever sat through a party you didn't really want to be at.

input: Okay, so this is the outline for the blog post about our washing machine dying in the middle of a cycle. I want to keep it practical, and I've thought about the order already, so let me just go through it. The working title is "The Night the Washer Stopped Mid-Spin." It's going on the family blog under the household section, and the audience is mostly people who've never had to deal with an appliance repair and are panicking about it the way we did. I want the tone to be calm and a little dry, not dramatic. Opening paragraph. Start with the facts. It was Thursday, the fourteenth of March, around seven in the evening. Our washer is a Bosch front loader we bought secondhand in 2019 from a woman named Ruth Okonkwo in Redfern, for two hundred and forty dollars. It had been running a heavy load of towels when it made a grinding noise, then stopped with the drum still full of water and the door locked. That detail matters, so I'll say it plainly: the door was locked and the display read E15. Second section, what I checked first. I did not panic-call anyone. I looked up the error code in the manual, which was tucked in the drawer under the dryer. E15 means the water level sensor or the drain pump, and the manual suggests checking the drain filter first. So I put a shallow baking tray and two old beach towels on the floor, unscrewed the filter at the bottom corner, and got about four litres of grey water out. Nothing blocking it except a single hair tie and a coin my son swears he didn't put in there. Third section, what didn't work. I restarted it, held the power button for ten seconds as the manual said, and the same code came back. I tried a drain-only cycle. The pump hummed and nothing moved. That pointed away from the filter and toward the pump itself or its wiring. I was not going to open the back panel with the plug still in, so I unplugged it at the wall and waited an hour. Fourth section, calling the repairer. I rang Coastline Appliance Service the next morning, Friday the fifteenth. The technician, Marco Delgado, was booked for the following Tuesday, the nineteenth, between eight and noon. His call-out fee was eighty-five dollars, which he said would be waived if the repair went ahead. I want readers to know to ask that question up front. Fifth section, the diagnosis and the cost. Marco arrived on time, pulled the back panel, and found the drain pump had a cracked housing and a seized impeller. The replacement pump was one hundred and ten dollars plus labour for an hour and a half. Total, including parts and the waived call-out, came to one hundred and sixty-two dollars. I'll compare that honestly against the cost of a new machine, roughly nine hundred dollars for the same capacity, and say it was the right call for a machine that otherwise ran well. Closing section. Two practical tips: keep the manual somewhere you'll find it, and clean the drain filter every few months, because it's the cheapest thing you can do to avoid a midnight scare. I'll end with a photo of the tray full of grey water and a line about how the towels finally got washed on the Wednesday at the laundromat on Cleveland Street.

I've already ordered them from Halden Building Supplies, and they're delivering on Friday afternoon between two and four. That's sixty bricks, reclaimed London stock to match the old ones as closely as possible, plus two bags of lime mortar, not cement. Bed them on a thin layer of mortar and make sure they overhang the face by about two centimetres on both sides, so rainwater runs off and not down the brick. Last thing. Tomasz, if you read this before Saturday, please bring your own gloves and the good trowel, not the orange one, which is rusty. I'll bring lunch and the flask. That's everything. I'll record a follow-up once the wall's up.

input: Okay, so I've been meaning to record this for a while, because I finished the book last Sunday and I still haven't stopped thinking about it. It's called "The Long Way Down the Ridge," by a woman named Marisol Ferreira, and it's basically a memoir about the four days she spent hiking the Cascade Traverse with her brother Teo back in August 2009. I picked it up at the library in Bellingham mostly because the cover looked nice, and I did not expect to be crying on the bus. What got me first was how ordinary the setup is. They're not climbing anything dramatic. They're just two siblings who haven't really talked since their dad's funeral, carrying packs that are way too heavy, arguing about who forgot the water filter. Ferreira is so good at the small stuff, like the blisters, the way the light changes at four in the afternoon, the smell of wet cedar after a rain. The middle section is where it really got to me. Teo has this moment on the second night, near a lake she names Halcyon Tarn, where he admits he's been planning to move to Alaska and never told anyone. She doesn't try to fix it or give some big speech. She just makes him coffee on the little stove and lets the silence sit there. I read that passage three times. I think I've been that sister, honestly, and I've been that brother too. Now, is it a perfect book? No. The last fifty pages get a little tidy, and there's a flashback chapter about their mother that felt like it belonged in a different book. But I didn't mind, because the core of it is so honest. So if you've got a long weekend coming up and somebody in your life you've been meaning to call, I'd grab this one. Maybe bring two water filters, just in case.

input: Okay, so this is a walkthrough of the problem we've been having with the trail-logging app on the group hike last weekend. I've thought it through a bit, so I'll go in order: what happened, what we've already tried, and what I think we should do next. The app is called TrailTally, and Priya Raghunathan set it up on her phone before we left Fernhill car park on Saturday the fourteenth of September. The plan was simple. Each of us would have GPS tracking switched on, the app would record the route, and at the end we'd have a clean map of the whole loop for the club newsletter. That was the idea, anyway. What actually happened is that Priya's track recorded fine, but Dmitri Ocampo's and mine stopped logging around the four-kilometre mark, just after the stile below Hollin Crag. Both of our tracks just end there. No error message, no crash that either of us noticed. The app still showed "recording" on our screens until we got back to the car, so we only found out afterwards when we opened the summary. So the first thing I did on Sunday evening was check the obvious stuff. Battery saver was off on both phones. Background app refresh was allowed. Location permission was set to "Always" rather than "While using," which I'd been told is a common cause. None of that changed anything when I reset the settings and tested it on my kitchen table, because the tracking worked fine indoors, which tells us nothing about the hillside. On Monday I went out for a short test walk along the canal towpath, about two kilometres, with the phone in my jacket pocket the way we'd carried it on the hike. It logged the whole way. That was encouraging, but it also made me think the problem might be signal-related rather than a settings issue, because the towpath is flat, open and has clear sky. The hillside below the crag is mostly shaded by trees and there's a valley that dips down there. Dmitri tried a different angle on Tuesday. He reinstalled the app completely, cleared its cache, and went out to the same stretch of the Fernhill path again with his phone in a chest pocket instead of a side pocket. His track held for nearly six kilometres before cutting out at a different point, near the reservoir gate. So the placement might matter, or it might be coincidence, and we can't tell from one run. Where I've landed is this. I don't think it's a single bug. It looks like the app drops tracking when GPS fix quality falls below a threshold and doesn't recover on its own, and that's a known limitation the support forum mentions for older Android builds. Dmitri's phone is on an older version, which fits. What I'd suggest for next time is three things. First, update everyone to the current build before we go. Second, switch to "Always" location access and keep phones in an outside pocket where they can see the sky. Third, and this is the important one, check the track status every hour at the stops, rather than trusting the recording indicator. If a track has stopped, we can at least note it and carry on with a paper map reference. I'll post the forum thread link in the group chat tonight, and I'll ask Priya whether she can send us her full export so we can compare timestamps. That's everything I've got for now.

input: Okay, so I wanted to talk through the podcast I listened to on the drive back from my sister's place last weekend. What stayed with me was how much of the episode was about the boring decisions. They spent almost three weeks just on the cabinet layout, and Teresa said the moment she stopped thinking about the island and started thinking about where the dishwasher door would hit someone's knee was the moment the plan actually got good. I think that's right. Most renovation advice focuses on finishes, and they barely mentioned tile. I also appreciated that they were honest about the money. The original budget was 38,000 dollars and they finished at 46,500, mostly because the subfloor under the old linoleum was rotted near the back door. Marcus didn't pretend that was a surprise. He said they'd set aside a fifteen percent buffer precisely because older houses hide things, and that the buffer was the only reason they didn't panic. If I'm honest, the episode made me want to do my own kitchen, which is probably the point. I'm going to start by measuring the room properly and writing down what annoys me every day. That feels like the sensible first step, and I'm glad I heard it from people who clearly learned it the hard way.

input: Okay, so I want to talk through the podcast episode I listened to last week, and then how it connects to the volunteer day we ran at the food bank on Saturday the fourteenth of September. I'd planned to take notes as I listened, so I'll go in order. The episode was called "Forty Hands" and it was hosted by a woman named Priya Lankford, who interviewed three coordinators from community pantries in the Midlands. What stuck with me was her first guest, Dev Okonkwo, who runs a pantry out of a converted church hall in Stourbridge. He said that the biggest failure most volunteer days have isn't a lack of people, it's a lack of jobs that people can see the end of. I wrote that down because it's exactly what went wrong for us the first time we ran the event, two years ago. So that's the frame I took into Saturday. Before anyone arrived, I split the day into four fixed stations: sorting donations, packing boxes, the intake desk, and loading the van for the Wednesday deliveries. Each station had a laminated card with a start point, an end point, and a rough count. Nobody was asked to "just help out." It worked better than I expected. Thirty-one people came, including a group of sixth formers from Hollins Academy led by Mrs. Tanya Reyes, and we packed 412 boxes by half past one. The part I'd like to remember is that the intake desk, which I'd assumed would be the dullest job, ended up being the one people asked to stay on. Dev's episode had said something similar, that people want to be useful to a person, not just to a process. If I'm honest, there are things I'd change. The van station ran short on tape, and I should have checked the stock on Friday night rather than trusting last month's list. I'll note that for next time, along with the fact that the sixth formers need a separate briefing. Overall the episode gave me a vocabulary for something I'd been doing by instinct, and the day gave me a test of it. That's a useful pairing, and I'm going to write both into the planning notes before the November event.

Turns out it was the whole of Eastfield, about eleven thousand homes according to the council's website.

The utility company, Northline Power, put up a notice saying they expected repairs by Thursday morning. input: Okay, so I finished the book about the Halvorsen garden last week, and I've been trying to figure out why it stuck with me. It's a memoir by a woman named Ingrid Vale, who inherited her grandmother's plot outside Duluth, Minnesota, in the spring of 2009. The garden was about a third of an acre, and by the time Ingrid got to it, the raspberry canes had taken over the whole east fence. What got me was how she writes about the first year. She didn't really know what she was doing. She planted sweet peas in April, which, I mean, you're supposed to do that in March or even earlier, and she admits she lost almost all of them to a late frost. She says she sat on the back step and cried about it, and then went to the hardware store on Cedar Avenue and bought a soil thermometer. I thought that was such a specific, human detail. There's a chapter about her grandmother's notebooks. Ingrid found forty-one of them in a cedar chest, all dated, going back to 1964. Every entry is just a line or two. "Beans up, June 3, cold night." "Lost the Brandywine to blight, Aug 19." And Ingrid started reading them the way you'd read a diary, except the diary was about tomatoes. Actually, no, it's more like a diary about patience. That's the thing I keep coming back to. Near the end she says the garden was never really finished, and that's the point. She stopped trying to make it look like the one in her grandmother's photographs and started just paying attention to what was actually growing there. I think that's the lesson, or at least the one I took. Anyway, I'm going to go out this weekend and see whether the sweet peas survived the winter in my own yard. Probably not, but I'm going to check.

The place I'm going to is Velo Nook on Tanner Street, about four miles from the flat. They're open Tuesday to Saturday, nine till six, and they don't take walk-ins for anything with a wheel off, so I'll book. I already checked and they have a slot on Wednesday the nineteenth at ten-fifteen. Wednesday works because I'm working from home that day and I can get across town before lunch.

Getting there is the bit I need to be careful about.

I can ride it, but if the gears are dodgy I'd rather not risk it on Hadley Road, which has the big hill and the lorries. So I'll put the bike on the car rack. The rack is in the garage, and the car is a silver Corolla with a full tank, so I don't need to stop for fuel on the way. I'll leave at nine-forty to give myself a buffer, because the parking behind the shop is only two spaces and I don't want to be circling.

If the quote comes in over that, I'll ask them to tell me what's essential and what can wait. The derailleur itself is probably the main cost, and I'd rather replace the cable and hanger too while they're in there, so I'm going to tell them that upfront rather than have them phone me about extras.

Then I need to plan for the gap.

I'll get the bus from Tanner Street back toward the centre. The number forty-two stops right outside the shop every twenty minutes, and the journey is around twenty-five minutes. I've got my transit card topped up, so there's nothing to organise there. I'll use the time to pick up the shopping at the Co-op on Albion Road, which is on the same route.

Last check before I hang up on this. Bike at the shop Wednesday morning, quote by Wednesday afternoon, budget of one forty, collection Thursday, ride on Saturday. Car rack is in the garage, the card is topped up, and Priya knows.

I think that covers it.

Okay, that's the plan.

input: Okay, so I'm going to walk through what's been going on with the budgeting app, because I think I finally know what's wrong with it. My sister Dana set it up for our household grocery budget back in March, and at first it was great. We'd put in two hundred and forty dollars a week, and it would tell us how much was left every time we scanned a receipt. Then, around the middle of May, the numbers started drifting. Our Thursday trip to Harmon's Market would show up as eighty-two dollars when the receipt said ninety-six, and the weekly total kept climbing even though we weren't buying more. Dana thought it was a sync problem, so she logged out and back in on her phone on May 14th. That didn't fix it. Next she tried deleting the Harmon's category and recreating it from scratch. That helped for about two days, and then the same gap came back. I reinstalled the app on my tablet on May 19th, thinking maybe the old data was corrupted, and the tablet showed the exact same wrong totals. So it's not one device. What finally clicked for me was the coupons. Harmon's started doing digital coupons through their loyalty card around the first of June, and the app is reading the discount as a separate line item and subtracting it twice. I checked three receipts from the second week of June, and every one had a single coupon that the app counted as two. Once I saw that, the drift made sense, because the bigger our coupon haul, the bigger the error. So here's where we are. Dana's going to contact support with the three receipts, and I'm going to start turning off the auto-import for coupon lines and entering those manually for the next few weeks. We'll see whether the totals line up with the bank statement at the end of June. If they do, I'll feel a lot better about trusting this thing again.
